‘Billionaire tax’ Prop 40 and its rival props 41 and 42
We dive deep into Prop 40 and its rival props, 41 and 42, and what's at stake.
Proposition 41 would make it harder to pass new special taxes in California. It would require the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters, and it would count any new special tax that voters approve toward the state’s spending cap.
Opponents of Prop. 40, the proposed “billionaire tax,” (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-prop-40-billionaire-tax) placed this measure on the ballot.
What’s at stake
This measure would make it more difficult to raise taxes in the future.
Here’s how it would work: If successful, Prop. 41 would require the state auditor to assess any proposed new taxes. Before any public vote, the auditor would identify ways the program set to benefit from the tax increase could cut its spending by at least 10% each year. A summary of this audit would appear in the information guide that’s mailed to voters. Prop. 41 would also require new special taxes to count toward California’s spending cap.
Prop. 41 directly undermines Prop. 40 (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-prop-40-billionaire-tax), the proposed wealth tax on billionaires, which exempts its potential revenue from the spending cap. Both Prop. 41 and Prop. 42 (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-proposition-42) were backed by Building a Better California (https://www.buildingabetterca.org/), funded heavily by Google co-founder Sergey Brin. If either measure gets more votes than Prop. 40, Prop. 40 is canceled, even if it also passes.
Official title on the ballot: Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/index.htm) :
Nullifies state taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes.
What your vote means
A “yes” vote means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
A “no” vote means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
Understanding Prop. 41
Prop. 41 targets special taxes, which raise revenue for a specific purpose, such as infrastructure or healthcare.
If passed, Prop. 41 would prohibit new special taxes from exempting their revenue from the state’s spending limit, established by a 1979 ballot measure. Critics say such exemptions are a way to pour more tax money into state coffers while sidestepping the “Gann Limit.” (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-3-2026-general-election/proposition-41-audits) The Gann Limit is named after Paul Gann, an anti-tax activist, and it seeks to cap the amount of money the state can spend. (Its baseline is state spending in 1978-79 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/what-would-proposition-41-mean-for-california/), adjusted for inflation and population changes.) Whenever state revenues exceed this cap for two consecutive years, California must refund the excess directly to taxpayers and through education spending. This has only happened twice (https://apnews.com/article/california-health-coronavirus-pandemic-business-personal-taxes-228c115a231bcc8ec000c7445e83d8e7).
Watch the ballot cram session analysis
What supporters say
Supporters say key social programs aren’t getting enough money despite California’s high taxes. They argue the state auditor check would ensure programs that benefit from special taxes spend money wisely. They also want these taxes to count toward the state spending limit, which would make tax rebates to Californians more likely.
Notable supporters: Reform California, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu and Stewart Resnick, chairman and CEO of the Wonderful Company.
What opponents say
The chief opponent is SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, which sponsors Prop. 40. The union argues that Prop. 41 is designed to trick voters into blocking a wealth tax on billionaires without realizing it. It says the measure isn’t really about auditing waste in public programs, but is instead a way for billionaires to avoid paying a one-time tax on their wealth.
Notable opponents: SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the California Democratic Party, California State PTA and the American Civil Liberties Union of Southern California
Fiscal impact
If passed, Prop. 41 would increase costs for the state auditor. But those costs would depend on how many new special taxes are proposed and approved, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), which estimates these costs would likely start in the low millions of dollars per year and would grow over time.
Adding audit summaries to voter guides would increase printing and mailing costs by “a few hundred thousand dollars” per initiative, according to that same analysis. That breakdown also adds that Prop. 41 could bring savings by requiring the state auditor to recommend ways that programs can cut costs, although those savings “would depend on future decisions and are not known.”
Overall, the Legislative Analyst’s Office determined that the “net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers.”

Endorsement: Prop 41 is a cynical poison pill. And it isn’t the only one on California’s ballot
Prop 41 is one of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
It wouldn’t be a California election without a few petty, revenge-motivated ballot measures.
Proposition 41 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop41-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is one of two poison pill attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax. The measure explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 41 or its cousin initiative Prop 42 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-proposition-42-taxes-22449389.php) pass with a larger number of votes.
Backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php), Prop 41 would require new special taxes that raise money for specific purposes to adhere to state spending rules, while mandating regular audits of the programs they fund.

But they’re largely redundant and would decrease efficiency.

Below are the League of Women Voters of California’s recommendations ** on the propositions appearing on the November 3, 2026 ballot. We base our recommendations on League positions developed through study and member consensus, and the LWVC Board of Directors carefully reviews each measure before taking a position.
**The LWVC Education Fund has provided an unbiased explanation of each ballot measure to help voters make informed decisions. Visit the link at the end of each recommendation for more about each measure.
Proposition 1
VETERANS & AFFORDABLE HOUSING BONDS
Funding from the 2018 bond for broad affordable housing programs has been spent, and there is a corresponding backlog of affordable housing projects stuck waiting for years for financing. Many families in California continue to endure high housing costs, leading to an increase in homelessness and overcrowding. Public subsidy is necessary to provide safe and stable housing for households at the lowest incomes.
Prop 1 authorizes $10 billion in general obligation bonds for the construction, acquisition, rehabilitation, and preservation of affordable housing and for homeownership programs, plus $1.25 billion, also in general obligation bonds, for veteran mortgage assistance through the CalVet Home Loan Program, expected to be repaid from borrowers’ mortgage payments.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 1 Campaign (https://yesonprop1ca.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 1 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-1/)
Proposition 2
SAVE FOR CALIFORNIA’S FUTURE ACT
Proposition 2 will allow California to save more money during strong economic years so it can protect schools and other essential services when revenues fall.
California’s budget can change dramatically from one year to the next. The state relies heavily on personal income taxes, including taxes on capital gains. Capital gains are profits people earn when they sell stocks, businesses, real estate, or other investments. These taxes bring in much more money when financial markets are doing well, but that revenue can disappear quickly during an economic downturn.
Prop 2 would help California prepare for those swings. It would allow the state to build a larger rainy-day fund and require it to save more when capital gains revenues are unusually high. That would give California a stronger financial cushion during recessions, natural disasters, public health emergencies, and other difficult periods.
Saving more during good years can help prevent deep cuts to public services during bad years. It can also reduce the need for emergency borrowing and other painful budget actions.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 2 Campaign (https://www.yesonprop2.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 2 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-2/)
Proposition 3
CHILDREN’S EDUCATION & HEALTH CARE PROTECTION
Proposition 3 would protect funding for schools, health care, and other essential services by keeping California’s current income tax rates on the highest-income 2 percent of taxpayers. Without Prop 3, those rates would fall in 2031, reducing state revenue by an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion each year. Prop 3 would not change anyone’s tax rate today.
About 40 percent of this revenue goes to schools and community colleges. The rest helps fund Medi-Cal and other health and human services, other essential public services, and state budget reserves.
California should not give its highest-income residents a multi-billion-dollar tax cut while schools, health care, and other essential services face serious financial pressure. Prop 3 simply asks the top 2 percent to keep paying the same rates they already pay. The League strongly supports the measure because it protects vital services, helps California weather economic downturns, and keeps the state’s tax system fair.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 3 Campaign (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 3 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-3/)
Proposition 4
CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT
Elections should be won, not bought. But in California, personal wealth and access to big donors have become unofficial qualifications for public office. Qualified candidates without wealthy networks are often shut out before voters hear their ideas, while candidates and officeholders spend too much time chasing large checks.
Prop 4 gives Californians a way to change that. It lifts California’s near-total ban on public campaign financing and allows the state and local governments to create voluntary programs. The measure creates no financing program and provides no campaign funding by itself. Each jurisdiction decides whether to adopt a program and how to design and pay for it.
Public financing can make small donations matter more, give candidates without personal fortunes a fairer chance to compete, and let them spend more time listening to voters. By reducing the advantage of incumbents, wealthy donors, and special interests, these programs can make elections more open, competitive, and accountable.
They can also open the door to candidates who better reflect California. Latino, Asian American or Pacific Islander, and Black Californians make up nearly two-thirds of our population but remain vastly underrepresented in local government across much of the state. High campaign costs help keep that barrier in place. When voters can choose candidates who understand their communities and reflect their interests, they have more reason to participate.
Prop 4 protects public money. Candidates must show broad grassroots support and agree to spending limits. Money reserved for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used. Programs cannot favor incumbents or discriminate by party. Public funds cannot pay legal defense costs or fines or repay a candidate’s personal loan to a campaign. Finally, the measure triples the maximum fine for illegal foreign money in California elections.
Prop 4 gives every California community the freedom to build elections where voters have more power and wealthy donors and special interests have less.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 4 Campaign (https://www.cafairelections.org/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 4 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-4/)
Proposition 5
RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS
California’s recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official. It should never become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a small fraction of voters. However, that is exactly what today’s recall rules allow, since the same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets the most votes, even if that’s far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process. Voters are asked to remove an officer by majority vote, then hand that same office to a replacement chosen by whomever gets the most votes, often in a field crowded with dozens of candidates and with no requirement that the winner reach half the vote. That’s a loophole that can easily be exploited. In 2021, had the recall against Governor Newsom succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with the support of just 28% of recall voters, a stark illustration of exactly this problem.
Prop 5 restores the recall to its proper purpose: deciding whether an official should remain in office. It shuts down that back door with one clean fix: removing the replacement candidate vote from the recall ballot itself. If a recall succeeds, the vacancy is filled through succession, appointment, or a later election decided by real majority support. These are the same rules used to fill any other vacancy in state government. A recalled officer can still run again later. This is a pro-democracy safeguard too – the choice stays with voters rather than being taken away entirely. What Prop 5 rules out is any return to office through appointment, so a recalled officer can only reclaim the seat by winning a real vote.
This is a matter of basic fairness and majority rule. Prop 5 protects accountability while ending a system that can hand power to a candidate most voters never chose.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Yes on Prop 5 Campaign (https://fixtherecall.com/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 5 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-5/)
Proposition 37
LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF NEW HOMES
California must build more homes and make homeownership possible for more families. The League of Women Voters of California has worked toward those goals for decades and supports Prop 1, which would provide $10 billion for affordable housing and homeownership programs and $1.25 billion for veterans’ home loans.
Prop 37 addresses a real barrier: the down payment. But it does so by adding a second mortgage that buyers generally would repay every month.
Prop 37 could help a family buy a home without making it affordable to keep. Buyers generally would repay the Prop 37 loan each month in addition to their first mortgage, property taxes, insurance, repairs, and other costs. Voters would not know the interest rate, loan term, or monthly payment before approving the program.
The program could reinforce racial and economic gaps instead of targeting families facing the greatest barriers . Generations of housing discrimination have left many Black and Latino families with less wealth to draw on, but Prop 37 gives no priority to first-time or first-generation buyers and does not exclude current or former homeowners. Households earning up to twice the area median income could qualify, including some earning more than $300,000 a year, while buyers would still have to provide at least 3 percent of the home price.
The program is not tied to good planning. Assistance could be used only for newly built or newly converted homes, with no requirement that they be near jobs, transit, schools, or services or avoid areas with high transportation, insurance, or natural-hazard costs.
Too much remains undecided. The Legislative Analyst says it is uncertain whether investors would buy the bonds, how the loans would compare in cost with other assistance, or whether the program would result in more homes being built or purchased. The interest rate and repayment terms would be set after the election.
California needs homeownership programs that lower families’ total costs, confront racial barriers to building wealth, and support strong communities. Prop 37 does not meet that test.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 37 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-37/)
Proposition 38
BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH
Medical research can save lives, but Prop 38 is the wrong way to fund it. It would authorize $8.4 billion in borrowing for immunology and immunotherapy research and require the state to make $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for about 20 years. Those payments would come from the General Fund, which also pays for schools, health care, and other public services.
Borrowing is a poor way to pay for ongoing scientific research. Bonds are best suited to long-lived investments such as buildings and infrastructure. With interest, the Legislative Analyst estimates Prop 38 would cost about 10 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the research up front.
Prop 38 would lock billions of dollars into one field of research for years to come. About half of the money would go to a single UC-affiliated research institute and the other half to a grant program, with at least $4.2 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research. Scientific opportunities and public health needs change. State funding should be able to respond to those changes rather than locking billions of dollars into one field of research through a ballot measure.
Research royalties are no reason to take on $8.4 billion in debt. When voters approved $3 billion for stem-cell research in 2004, supporters pointed to royalties and millions in new state revenue. By 2022, CIRM reported only $15.6 million in its licensing and royalties fund from royalty payments. Prop 38 again points to research-generated revenue as a way to offset public costs, but the Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing are unknown.
California can support important medical research without committing taxpayers to decades of debt and restricting future choices about where limited public dollars can do the most good.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
No on Prop 38 Campaign (https://votenoonprop38.org/)
Unbiased Explanation: Prop 38 (https://cavotes.org/ballot-measure/2026-prop-38/)
Proposition 39
PROHIBITS VOTING WITHOUT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED ID
Prop 39 is a partisan power grab to further President Trump’s voter suppression efforts. It is based on lies about our elections. Prop 39 is intended to make it harder to vote and easier for politicians to decide which voters count. Right-wing billionaires spent millions to put it on the ballot.
California’s elections are already secure. Voters swear to citizenship under penalty of perjury, and officials verify identity at registration, check the rolls in person, and match every mail ballot signature.
A new registration hurdle. Millions of existing voters could be forced to effectively re-register to “designate” a government ID for mail voting, like a driver’s license or Social Security number.
Identity theft risk. You would be required to put the last four digits of that sensitive ID number on the outside of your ballot envelope – next to your name, address, and signature.
Valid ballots thrown out. Your mailed ballot would not be counted if the number you wrote didn’t match the “designated” number. One wrong digit or a blank field could sink a valid ballot, with no guaranteed notice or chance to fix it. Texas tried this and rejected one in eight mail ballots. Those voters were less likely to vote again.
An ID check every time you vote in person. You would have to show a government-issued ID every time, even after officials verified who you are. Most voters turned away under similar laws elsewhere had qualifying ID, just not on them.
A modern-day poll tax. A “free” ID is not free. Getting one costs transportation, childcare, time off work, and fees for the paperwork behind it. Seniors, students, low-income workers, voters with disabilities, and voters of color are hit hardest.
Valid ID still must match. Nearly 30 percent of U.S. adults have changed their name, 94 percent of them women. Californians who took a new name at marriage, and transgender voters whose documents lag may hold valid ID and be turned away anyway.
Bad data and wrongful purges. Citizenship checks would likely run through untrustworthy federal databases that wrongly flag eligible citizens to purge them from voter rolls.
Longer lines and slower results. Extra ID checks and flagged ballots add delay, and the lawsuits would stretch it further, handing election deniers more time to spread lies.
Hundreds of millions of dollars every year. New systems, staffing, free ID cards, audits, and lawsuits, all paid for while California already has budget problems.
Don’t let President Trump and right-wing billionaires decide whose vote counts.
LWVC RECOMMENDS:
No on Prop 39 Campaign (https://noonprop39.com/)

CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT
Elections should be won, not bought. But in California, personal wealth and access to big donors have become unofficial qualifications for public office. Qualified candidates without wealthy networks are often shut out before voters hear their ideas, while candidates and officeholders spend too much time chasing large checks.
Prop 4 gives Californians a way to change that. It lifts California’s near-total ban on public campaign financing and allows the state and local governments to create voluntary programs. The measure creates no financing program and provides no campaign funding by itself. Each jurisdiction decides whether to adopt a program and how to design and pay for it.
Public financing can make small donations matter more, give candidates without personal fortunes a fairer chance to compete, and let them spend more time listening to voters. By reducing the advantage of incumbents, wealthy donors, and special interests, these programs can make elections more open, competitive, and accountable.
They can also open the door to candidates who better reflect California. Latino, Asian American or Pacific Islander, and Black Californians make up nearly two-thirds of our population but remain vastly underrepresented in local government across much of the state. High campaign costs help keep that barrier in place. When voters can choose candidates who understand their communities and reflect their interests, they have more reason to participate.
Prop 4 protects public money. Candidates must show broad grassroots support and agree to spending limits. Money reserved for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used. Programs cannot favor incumbents or discriminate by party. Public funds cannot pay legal defense costs or fines or repay a candidate’s personal loan to a campaign. Finally, the measure triples the maximum fine for illegal foreign money in California elections.
Prop 4 gives every California community the freedom to build elections where voters have more power and wealthy donors and special interests have less.

Proposition 5
RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS
California’s recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official. It should never become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a small fraction of voters. However, that is exactly what today’s recall rules allow, since the same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets the most votes, even if that’s far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process. Voters are asked to remove an officer by majority vote, then hand that same office to a replacement chosen by whomever gets the most votes, often in a field crowded with dozens of candidates and with no requirement that the winner reach half the vote. That’s a loophole that can easily be exploited. In 2021, had the recall against Governor Newsom succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with the support of just 28% of recall voters, a stark illustration of exactly this problem.
Prop 5 restores the recall to its proper purpose: deciding whether an official should remain in office. It shuts down that back door with one clean fix: removing the replacement candidate vote from the recall ballot itself. If a recall succeeds, the vacancy is filled through succession, appointment, or a later election decided by real majority support. These are the same rules used to fill any other vacancy in state government. A recalled officer can still run again later. This is a pro-democracy safeguard too – the choice stays with voters rather than being taken away entirely. What Prop 5 rules out is any return to office through appointment, so a recalled officer can only reclaim the seat by winning a real vote.
This is a matter of basic fairness and majority rule. Prop 5 protects accountability while ending a system that can hand power to a candidate most voters never chose.

Proposition 37
LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF NEW HOMES
California must build more homes and make homeownership possible for more families. The League of Women Voters of California has worked toward those goals for decades and supports Prop 1, which would provide $10 billion for affordable housing and homeownership programs and $1.25 billion for veterans’ home loans.
Prop 37 addresses a real barrier: the down payment. But it does so by adding a second mortgage that buyers generally would repay every month.
Prop 37 could help a family buy a home without making it affordable to keep. Buyers generally would repay the Prop 37 loan each month in addition to their first mortgage, property taxes, insurance, repairs, and other costs. Voters would not know the interest rate, loan term, or monthly payment before approving the program.
The program could reinforce racial and economic gaps instead of targeting families facing the greatest barriers . Generations of housing discrimination have left many Black and Latino families with less wealth to draw on, but Prop 37 gives no priority to first-time or first-generation buyers and does not exclude current or former homeowners. Households earning up to twice the area median income could qualify, including some earning more than $300,000 a year, while buyers would still have to provide at least 3 percent of the home price.
The program is not tied to good planning. Assistance could be used only for newly built or newly converted homes, with no requirement that they be near jobs, transit, schools, or services or avoid areas with high transportation, insurance, or natural-hazard costs.
Too much remains undecided. The Legislative Analyst says it is uncertain whether investors would buy the bonds, how the loans would compare in cost with other assistance, or whether the program would result in more homes being built or purchased. The interest rate and repayment terms would be set after the election.
California needs homeownership programs that lower families’ total costs, confront racial barriers to building wealth, and support strong communities. Prop 37 does not meet that test.

Proposition 38
BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH
Medical research can save lives, but Prop 38 is the wrong way to fund it. It would authorize $8.4 billion in borrowing for immunology and immunotherapy research and require the state to make $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for about 20 years. Those payments would come from the General Fund, which also pays for schools, health care, and other public services.
Borrowing is a poor way to pay for ongoing scientific research. Bonds are best suited to long-lived investments such as buildings and infrastructure. With interest, the Legislative Analyst estimates Prop 38 would cost about 10 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the research up front.
Prop 38 would lock billions of dollars into one field of research for years to come. About half of the money would go to a single UC-affiliated research institute and the other half to a grant program, with at least $4.2 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research. Scientific opportunities and public health needs change. State funding should be able to respond to those changes rather than locking billions of dollars into one field of research through a ballot measure.
Research royalties are no reason to take on $8.4 billion in debt. When voters approved $3 billion for stem-cell research in 2004, supporters pointed to royalties and millions in new state revenue. By 2022, CIRM reported only $15.6 million in its licensing and royalties fund from royalty payments. Prop 38 again points to research-generated revenue as a way to offset public costs, but the Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing are unknown.
California can support important medical research without committing taxpayers to decades of debt and restricting future choices about where limited public dollars can do the most good.

**Gann Limits**, a form of appropriations limit, are caps on government budgets in California.
These caps apply to the state government of California and to local governments like cities and school districts.
Gann Limits forbid governments from spending more than a certain amount per year.
They also forbid governments from bringing in more tax revenue than they would be allowed to spend.
With some exceptions, a government that brings in too much tax revenue over a two-year period is required to cut taxes for future years.

Proposition 41
Require audits of new tax programs
This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. The auditor would assess whether the program that would receive funding could cut spending by at least 10% annually. Any new special tax approved by voters would count toward California’s spending limit, potentially triggering automatic refunds that reduce funding for other state programs. If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes. It was placed on the ballot by opponents of the proposed billionaire tax.

Supporters say key social programs are not getting enough funding despite California’s high taxes. They argue the state auditor should assess whether the programs that would benefit from special taxes are spending money wisely. Supporters also want these special taxes to count toward the state spending limit, making tax rebates to Californians more likely.

The chief opponent is SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the sponsor of Proposition 40. The union argues that Prop. 41 is designed to trick voters into unknowingly blocking a wealth tax on billionaires. Prop. 41 isn’t about auditing waste in public programs, the union says; instead it’s a way for billionaires to avoid paying taxes once on their huge wealth.

PROP 41: Special-Tax Audits and the Spending-Limit Lock
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2041.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Summary
Proposition 41 would write two rules into the California Constitution. First, programs funded by new state special taxes would face independent audits by the state auditor. These audits would occur when the ballot initiative is initially proposed and then every four years after a special tax takes effect. Second, no new state tax could circumvent the Gann limit, the voter-approved spending cap adopted in 1979. Hoover Institution research shows that California’s spending has grown far faster than inflation or population and that the state budget rises and falls with the fortunes of a small number of high-income taxpayers. Proposition 41 is best read as an attempt to restore discipline to that budget. It also contains a clause that, if it outpolls Proposition 40, would void the billionaire tax on the same ballot (see California Decides, Prop 40: The Billionaire Tax Act (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-40)).
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues from State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0040A1).
Type: Initiated constitutional amendment.
A vote YES means: Starting retroactively on January 1, 2026, any program that would be the recipient of new or increased special tax revenues as a result of a citizen initiative must undergo state performance audits prior to the vote. Such programs, and those receiving revenues from legislatively enacted new or increased special taxes, must be audited every four years thereafter. No new state tax or increase to a state tax enacted on or after that date may route its revenue outside California’s voter-approved spending limit, commonly referred to as the Gann limit.
A vote NO means: California keeps current law. New special taxes are not subject to this audit regime, and new taxes may continue to direct revenue into funds that sit outside the Gann limit, as several existing taxes already do.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0040A1, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0040A1%20(Gov.%20Efficiency).pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 25-0040 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-040)
1. Overview
Proposition 41 would add a new Article XXIV, titled “Protecting Taxpayer Dollars,” to the California Constitution. It has two main provisions.
The first provision is an audit requirement for programs that would receive funds from proposed special tax initiatives. A special tax is one whose revenue is dedicated to specific purposes rather than available for general use. When the proponents of a citizen initiative that would create a new or increased special tax notify the secretary of state that they have gathered 25 percent of the required signatures, the state auditor must begin a financial and performance audit of each program the special tax would fund. The audit must assess program effectiveness, evaluate the potential for fraud, waste, and abuse, and recommend ways the program could achieve budgetary savings of at least 10 percent a year. If the measure qualifies for the ballot, an executive summary of the audit must be printed in the state voter information guide.
A subsequent audit must be repeated every four years for every new or increased special tax enacted by the legislature or by voters on or after January 1, 2026. When a tax passes, the audit costs are reimbursed from the tax’s own revenue. When a tax initiative fails to qualify or is rejected, the general fund absorbs the cost.
The second provision protects the state spending limit from being circumvented by future state taxes. The Gann limit, adopted by voters as Proposition 4 in 1979 and amended by Proposition 111 in 1990, caps how much tax revenue the state may appropriate each year. It’s adjusted for increases to population and per capita income, and some substantial categories of spending are excluded from the cap. According to the Gann limit, if tax revenue exceeds the limit over two consecutive years the excess revenue must be split between taxpayer rebates and additional K–14 school funding. For context, rapid tax revenue growth has rarely resulted in mandatory Gann limit rebates.
However, under current rules a new tax can be written to deposit its revenue in a fund that is excluded from the appropriations counted against the Gann limit. Proposition 41 would forbid that design for any state tax enacted by the legislature or by voter initiative, but the ban is limited to taxes that take effect on or after January 1, 2026. New special taxes would still be permitted, but their revenue would simply count toward the same spending cap that applies to other nonexempt tax revenues.
The second provision connects Proposition 41 to Proposition 40, the Billionaire Tax Act. If Prop 40 is approved it would route its revenue into a separate reserve fund that sits outside the structure of the Gann limit, the Proposition 98 school-funding guarantee, and the rainy-day budget rules. Proposition 41 prohibits new or increased state taxes from circumventing the structure intended to limit the growth of California government spending, and it includes specific text that will nullify Proposition 40 if both initiatives pass but Proposition 41 receives more yes votes.
2. The legal language
Full text:
Initiative 25-0040A1, “The Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0040A1%20(Gov.%20Efficiency).pdf) (eight pages, amended language submitted January 12, 2026).
Key language:
“No state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after January 1, 2026 shall be exempted or excluded from the Government Spending Limitation. The State of California shall not impose, collect, or enforce any state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after January 1, 2026 if the state tax is exempted or excluded from the Government Spending Limitation.”
What it amends: Adds a new Article XXIV, titled “Protecting Taxpayer Dollars,” to the California Constitution. The article defines “Government Spending Limitation” as Article XIII B, the Gann limit, and defines an exempted tax as one whose revenue is deposited outside the general fund and left out of the appropriations subject to the limit or that raises the appropriations limit by statute.
Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it. The measure also includes a self-defense provision that appoints and funds independent counsel through a continuous general fund appropriation if the governor and attorney general decline to defend it.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
What?
It would create constitutionally required audits of programs funded by new or increased special taxes, both before a tax initiative reaches voters and every four years after a tax takes effect. It also creates a ban on excluding the revenue from any new or increased state tax from the Gann spending limit.
Where?
Statewide, written into the California Constitution.
When?
It takes effect on passage and reaches back to taxes enacted or effective on or after January 1, 2026.
Why?
The initiative’s authors frame it as a response to California’s nation-leading tax rates and their effect on the state’s affordability crisis. The stated purpose is to require up-front, recurring audits of programs funded by special taxes and to prevent new taxes from circumventing the Gann limit so that surplus revenue is refunded rather than spent.
4. Analysis and Assessment
Audit requirements of Proposition 41 address a documented problem. For example, in 2024 the state auditor found that California spent roughly $24 billion on homelessness and housing programs over five fiscal years without consistently tracking whether the money reduced homelessness. Three of the five programs reviewed did not produce enough data to judge their cost-effectiveness at all. Proposition 41 would make that kind of review routine for programs funded by new special taxes, and it would give voters an audit summary before they vote on a tax initiative. Independent, recurring performance audits with concrete savings targets are the kind of accountability that good-government advocates across the spectrum have long sought.
Proposition 41’s requirement that future special taxes be subject to the Gann limit is similarly reasonable: California’s fiscal challenge is accelerated spending, not a shortage of revenue. Research by Hoover Institution Senior Fellow Lee Ohanian shows that from 2019 to 2023 California’s population fell by almost 500,000 people, while the state budget grew nearly 57 percent (31 percent after inflation). Additional research by Hoover fellows Lanhee J. Chen and Joshua D. Rauh describes how California’s heavy reliance on the personal income tax, which now supplies most general fund tax revenue, ties the budget to the performance of the stock market. In 2021, the top 10 percent of taxpayers paid almost 90 percent of personal income tax revenue. Meanwhile, the state budget swung $175 billion from a surplus in 2022 to a deficit in 2024.
The Gann limit is one of the few constitutional tools that restrains government spending growth during economic booms that becomes a fiscal catastrophe during leaner times. Prior analysis by Hoover Fellow Bill Whalen has traced how the Gann limit’s fiscal discipline has been eroded over time, from Proposition 111’s 1990 exclusion of new gas tax revenue to budgeting practices that kept billions out of the limit calculation. Proposition 41 would close the special-fund circumvention for any future tax.
Importantly, Prop 41 does not ban new taxes, nor does it cut existing programs. It simply requires that revenue from any new tax be counted alongside the rest of state spending, so that a future surplus is dedicated to a tax rebate and additional school funding (per Prop 4 and Prop 111) rather than accumulating in a dedicated fund. This rule should help encourage policymakers to be more thoughtful about expanding government programs when tax revenues unexpectedly increase.
Like Proposition 42, Proposition 41 contains a clause that, if it outpolls Proposition 40, would nullify Prop 40. This specificity is likely preferable to asking the courts to decide which parts of two conflicting constitutional amendments survive.
5. Conclusion
Proposition 41 would require any programs receiving funding from new or increased special taxes to be audited by the state auditor to assess performance, evaluate potential for waste, fraud, and abuse, and identify explicit cost savings opportunities. It would also require each new state tax enacted by the legislature or by voter initiative to be subject to the Gann limit. Its most immediate effect would be to nullify Proposition 40 if it draws more yes votes, while its lasting effect would be to hold all future state taxes to the same spending cap as the rest of the budget.
Hoover Institution research shows that California’s fiscal problem is driven by spending increases that have managed to outstrip even the state’s strong tax revenue growth. From that perspective, Proposition 41 would offer increased oversight on how well California is spending taxpayer dollars.

The most hotly debated initiative on the November ballot is Proposition 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires. As this Editorial Board opined (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/) in our opposition, the union-created Billionaire Tax Act would send a dangerous message to current and future entrepreneurs, and “have a chilling effect on investment.”
But two closely related measures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://www.bakersfield.com/opinion/our-view/our-view-vote-no-on-propositions-40-41-42-tax-propositions-hurt-state-californians/article_1c8492b8-5fb9-4897-9f1c-c9ba56460e0d.amp.html) , have received much less attention — partly because they’re so complicated. By adding related measures to the ballot, opponents of Prop. 40 are hoping that voters approve one of these alternatives that will derail Prop. 40. Because these two measures have elements that contradict Prop. 40, the one that gets the highest vote totals (if voters OK them all) would go into effect.
Adding similar-sounding measures also muddies the waters, thus increasing the likelihood that confused voters vote “no” on all of them — thus accomplishing the main goal of stopping the billionaires’ tax. But our goal isn’t to map out political strategies (https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/nash-game/) . It’s a worthy effort to try to stop a disastrous new tax scheme.
Besides their intended purpose of blocking Prop. 40, the measures could protect taxpayers for years to come.
Specifically, Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. Those audits, which must be completed before the initiative appears on the ballot, would be required to identify ways that such programs could cut annual costs by 10%, per an analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026) from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
While Prop. 40 exempts itself from state spending limits, Prop. 41 also requires new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit (https://www.sheehystrategygroup.com/news/2026/3/9/californias-state-appropriations-limit-gann-limit) — the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year. The state has passed a number of workarounds over the years, but applying new revenues to this formula would potentially require the return of certain additional tax revenues to taxpayers (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41) and the earmarking of revenues to infrastructure.
Prop. 42 is more straightforward. Per theLAO (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=42&year=2026), the initiative prohibits “new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.” California doesn’t currently tax the ownership of financial assets and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees), but the measure’s passage “could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes.” It also limits imposition of retroactive taxes.
So would the Editorial Board support these measures even if they were standalone initiatives? The answers are unequivocal: Yes and yes.

By Bay Area News Group Editorial Board (https://www.record-bee.com/author/bay-area-news-group-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: October 27, 2026 at 6:36 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Successive waves of federal cuts to California’s safety net are hitting our shores — and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. Its intentionally punitive and retaliatory cuts to California’s Medicaid program, Medi-Cal, are projected to cost the state billions of dollars per year and lead to more than a million Californians losing access to health care.
In the Bay Area, these cuts are becoming painful.
As our news organization documented this month, the number of uninsured people in emergency rooms at Santa Clara Valley Healthcare and Alameda Health System has spiked year over year.
Those county-run systems expect to collectively lose more than a billion dollars annually. Notably, while our systems and residents are scrambling to survive, rural America is receiving a $50 billion lifeline from House Republicans and President Trump to protect their health care systems.
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state’s safety net in the face of these devastating cuts.
However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40. And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 — countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state’s fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.
California has changed radically since the 1970s. And its fiscal rules must leave the state with the flexibility to address issues voters of the era never had to deal with — six-figure college costs, seven-figure mortgages and 13-figure wildfire costs.
The state must not surrender its future freedom of action to defeat a single, one-time tax proposal.
Proposition 42
This initiative would prohibit the state from taxing retroactively. And it would permanently ban the state from any new taxes on ownership of financial assets or other personal properties — think stocks, bonds, intellectual property, artwork, etc.
Taxes on wealth are rarely ideal, and our opposition to Proposition 40 reflects that.
However, we are witnessing an explosion of inequality, and the unpredictable course of AI’s development risks supercharging the gap between the haves and have-nots. Joint Venture Silicon Valley’s latest research shows that 78% of Bay Area residents are concerned AI will increase economic inequality.
Proposition 42 was written by this tech boom’s beneficiaries, who are now among the wealthiest humans in history. If this initiative had limited itself to nullifying Proposition 40, we could have supported it. However, amid this era’s technology- and climate-induced uncertainty, California must keep its options open.
Proposition 42 would needlessly and recklessly narrow them.
Reject Propositions 40, 41 and 42.

Prop
41
CA
Prop
41
|
Constitutional Amendment
Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes.
Requires audits of citizen initiatives for special taxes. Imposes spending limits on all new special taxes.
SPUR's Recommendation
More transparency and accountability in government spending are worthy objectives. However, the Legislative Analyst’s Office and the state auditor already have the authority to evaluate policies and programs to ensure they are equitable and efficient. Prop. 41 was primarily placed on the ballot to defeat Prop. 40, a measure to tax billionaires. In addition, it would constrain local and state governments’ ability to raise revenue now and in the future for much-needed housing, transportation, infrastructure, and social services, which are already facing cuts at the federal and state levels.
Vote NO
What Prop. 41 Would Do
Proposition 41 would require the state auditor, working with the Legislative Analyst’s Office, to conduct an independent review of any state-level citizen initiative that aims to create a new special tax once it reaches 25% of the required signature threshold to be placed on the ballot. (Special taxes differ from general taxes in that they dedicate revenue to a specific purpose.) All new state-level special taxes would be audited every four years.
Additionally, any new special taxes passed after January 1, 2026 — whether proposed through legislation or through voter initiatives — would be subject to the Gann Limit, a voter-imposed revenue spending limit explained in the Backstory section below.
The audit of proposed citizen initiatives would examine the individual programs that would receive funding through the special tax and assess whether the programs are sufficiently cost-efficient in their hiring and operating practices. It would recommend how the programs could save 10% of their costs. The audit information would be included in the voter information guide, which would increase printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per initiative, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
If a special tax passes, the state auditor would be required to conduct audits every four years to assess spending, evaluate efficiency, and recommend improvements. The auditor would consider public input when measuring the program’s effectiveness. The revenues generated would cover implementation costs. However, the state would pay the initial audit cost if voters rejected the special tax.
Prop. 41 is a countermeasure to the so-called billionaire tax, Prop. 40 (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/ca-prop-40-billionaire-tax). If both measures pass, the one receiving more votes would prevail.
The Backstory
Special taxes are taxes whose revenues are dedicated to a specific purpose rather than contributing to the state’s general fund budget. The State Legislature can levy special taxes with two-thirds voter approval, or an initiative placed on the ballot by voter signatures can do so with a simple majority (50% plus one vote). Currently, special taxes have no audit requirements or spending caps.
Since the late 1970s, California has faced numerous tax limitations through Prop. 13 and other constitutional amendments. The Gann Limit imposes requirements on how the state can spend General Fund revenues. If the state’s revenues exceed the Gann Limit — a dollar amount based on the state’s spending level in 1978–1979, adjusted for population and per capita income — half of revenues over the limit must be allocated to K–14 education and the other half returned to taxpayers. 1 Historically, the Gann Limit has rarely affected distribution of the state’s revenues, but if the state experiences strong income gains (including business/corporate/stock gains) over the limit, it could result in decreasing investment in state priorities such as housing, health care, economic development, and infrastructure.
The fiscal impacts of Prop. 41 are unknown. Adding pages to the voter information guide would cost money, but the audits could also create savings. If this measure prevents the state from raising new revenues from future taxes, it could have a significant negative fiscal impact in the longer term.
Prop. 41 is a countermeasure to Prop. 40, a one-time special tax on individuals with more than $1 billion in assets. Prop. 40 is intended to offset federal funding cuts to critical social safety net programs, including Medi-Cal, CalFresh, and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. The revenues generated from Prop. 40 would be exempt from the Gann Limit.
Prop. 41 was placed on the ballot through a signature-gathering effort led by Building a Better California, which is funded by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other billionaires. It requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass. If it passes with more votes than Prop. 40, it would nullify Prop. 40. (Building a Better California has also placed Prop. 42 (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/ca-prop-42-personal-property-taxes), a separate countermeasure to Prop. 40, on the ballot.)
Equity Impacts
Restricting spending from special taxes could negatively affect efforts to fund health care, food assistance, and other programs that disproportionately benefit lower-income Californians and communities of color.
Pro
Audits of proposed citizen initiatives could help ensure that the programs they would fund are cost-effective.
Cons
Prop. 41 was placed on the ballot to prevent a competing measure from succeeding. It could affect the state’s ability to raise revenue from other tax measures in the future.
Applying spending limits to new revenue measures could constrain local and state governments’ ability to fund urgent priorities amid unprecedented federal and state budget cuts.
Vote NO

Memorandum
To: Interested Parties
From: Brian Galle (UC Berkeley), David Gamage (University of Missouri), and Darien
Shanske (UC Davis)1
Re: Analysis of the Impacts of Propositions 41 and 42 on California’s Public Finance
Date: August 20, 2026
Introduction
In this memorandum, we will discuss the potential impacts of Propositions 41 and
42 on current and future initiatives and legislation, as well as on current California
Medicaid tax programs, starting with possible impacts on Proposition 3, the measure on
November’s ballot to extend personal income tax rate increases.
The purpose of the memo is to identify legal risks raised by the propositions that
prudent citizens should be aware of given the high stakes. We are not arguing how a court
should decide these issues and we do not claim that we are offering the best or most
persuasive legal arguments. We do, however, believe that there is a real risk courts could
reach these outcomes.
Our bottom line is that both propositions are poorly drafted in a manner that could
pose serious threats to California’s fiscal future, with the potential to undermine key
spending programs and potentially cause or worsen future budget crises. That is not
surprising. These are deceptive measures that were drafted quickly to trick voters that
support the billionaire wealth tax (Prop 40) into voting for competing measures that could
undermine that tax. The billionaire funders of these initiatives are acting with reckless
disregard for the collateral damage to California’s fiscal system and indeed they may even
benefit from weakening California’s existing taxes affecting the most wealthy.
Executive Summary
• The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could hamstring Proposition 3 (the
teacher-sponsored measure to fund education with taxes on million-dollar earners)
or invalidate it outright.
1 Institutional affiliations are listed for identification purposes only.
2
• The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could similarly hamstring many other
revenue raising measures, such as (for example) a tax on large employers who have
many employees on Medi-Cal.
• The prohibition on easing the state appropriation limit in Proposition 41 could
undermine many existing and proposed taxes to fund California’s contributions to
Medi-Cal, including current MCO taxes and the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee
(HQAF).
• The limitations on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could impact the
ability of the state to tax capital gains income, whether as part of Proposition 3 or
otherwise.
• The limitation on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could frustrate any
future attempt to reform California’s Vehicle License Fee, a backbone tool for
financing a wide array of local services.
Proposition 41
Proposition 41 makes two significant changes to California law. First, it adds many
new audit requirements, specifically pre-election audits of programs that would receive
funds from a proposed special tax initiative; and recurring audits, every four years, of
programs receiving moneys from special taxes enacted on or after January 1, 2026,
whether enacted by the Legislature or by initiative.2 Second, the proposition prohibits
collecting any state tax enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026 that is exempted
or excluded from the appropriations limit of Article XIIIB, the so-called Gann limit, whether
the exemption comes from an outside-the-General-Fund special fund whose spending is
not counted or from raising the limit itself. Proposition 41, secs. 3, 4(b). The obvious point
of this second change, hidden deep in the Proposition 41 text, is to nullify Proposition 40.
But both changes would likely weaken California public finance by threatening California’s
ability to raise revenues and fund spending programs.
On the Merits
Prop 41 targets the primary (and, in many cases, the only plausible remaining) way
that state tax policy can be done and that state services can be adequately funded. Any
increase in taxes enacted by the Legislature requires a two-thirds supermajority of each
house.3 Statewide initiatives, by contrast, can raise taxes by majority vote. Not surprisingly,
most major tax policy changes over recent decades have therefore occurred via initiative.
Since voters are unlikely to support tax increases for unspecified purposes, the limits on
2 Prop. 41, Secs. 1, 2.
3 Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(a).
3
measures adopting taxes for specified purposes tilts the deck against most of those
measures. Even if there were eventually an attempt to change Prop 41 through another
ballot measure, the pre-election audit requirement would still apply to any special tax
initiatives on that ballot.
The audits that Prop 41 would impose are slanted to make it more difficult to adopt
and fund new programs. Consider, for example, that a pre-election audit must consider:
“How the program's costs compare to any analogous programs in the non-government
sector”; and also: “Recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary
savings of at least 10% annually.” The audits would thus institutionalize a cost-cutting,
private-sector-comparison framework, and the executive summary of the pre-election
audit would be printed in the voter guide immediately after the Legislative Analyst’s
impartial analysis.4
In sum, every proposed special tax initiative would come before the voters bundled
with an official analysis oriented toward finding savings and private alternatives. These
expensive, burdensome and largely redundant5 requirements would hinder special tax
initiatives, making them more difficult to pass and less effective if passed.
The second provision regarding the Gann limit would double down on what has
proven to be a disastrous set of fiscal policies. The existing Gann limit works by capping
government expenditures over a given two-year period. Excess amounts must be split
between taxpayer rebates and education.6 The cap increases only to the extent of growth in
California population and cost of living.7 Given the increasing demands on the state
government, future uncertainties, and the changing nature of federal assistance, the limit
does not act so much as a ceiling as a vise squeezing out funds for core services.8 For
example, what happens if the state government needs to spend more on (say) wildfires? Or,

The state has hit the Gann limit recently (2022) and is about $30 billion under the

substantial increases in revenue. At that point, the state will be close to the limit. Any

Threats to Proposition 3
The audit requirements of Proposition 41 arguably apply to Proposition 3 because
Proposition 3 would seem to impose a “special tax” enacted “by a statewide initiative
measure on or after January 1, 2026.” Sec. 2(a)(1). Proposition 3 makes permanent the
existing 1% tax surcharge on income above $1 million that is set to expire in 2030; all of its
revenues are earmarked primarily for education. It thus likely involves a “special tax,”
which is “a tax that can only be used to fund specific, as opposed to unlimited, purposes”
(according to Prop 41), because the Education Protection Account revenues added by Prop
3 may be used only for specified education and health care purposes. Sec. 4(d) of
Proposition 41; Article XIII, Sec. 36(e) of Proposition 3.
As for whether Proposition 3 was enacted after January 1, 2026, a court could
plausibly find that a tax first approved in 2012 is “enacted” in 2026 when the voters delete
its sunset. The new provision is different than the old in that it will never expire; the post-
2030 tax will exist only because of the 2026 vote; and the adoption of the extension is itself
literally an enactment.9
Thus, Proposition 41 might plausibly be interpreted by courts as applying to
Proposition 3. If so, Proposition 41 would require onerous and burdensome audits of the
programs it funds.
Further, if both measures pass and Proposition 41 receives more affirmative votes,
every provision of Proposition 3, including the rate extension itself, could be ruled void.
The terms of Proposition 41 state that it nullifies other conflicting 2026 initiatives if it
receives more votes. Prop 41 defines conflicting measures as “another initiative measure

Threats to the MCO Tax
The sloppy drafting of Proposition 41 implicates policies far beyond Proposition 3.
We will briefly consider spending on health care.
Start with the Managed Care Organization (MCO) tax, which California expects to
generate as much as $8 billion annually in federal matching funds. There are now arguably
two separate MCO provisions that will take effect after 2026 authorization, both of them
threatened by Prop 41.
The first is SB 125, enacted in June 2026, which imposes a tax of $8.85 per enrollee
per month for 2027 through 2029 and deposits the proceeds in the new Medi-Cal Stability
Fund, dedicated to specified Medi-Cal purposes.11 SB 125 is a special tax enacted after
January 1, 2026, so under Prop 41 each Medi-Cal program receiving its moneys would face
recurring State Auditor financial and performance audits, with the private-sector
comparisons and ten percent savings recommendations, and with the Auditor reimbursed
from the tax revenues themselves.12 As explained above, this would be very burdensome
and problematic. And because the Stability Fund broadly co-funds managed care payments
and rates, there is a further risk that a court would rule that the auditable “programs”
include major portions of Medi-Cal managed care, rather than just the marginal SB 125
dollars. Thus Prop 41 could require the state to pay for audits recommending how to
privatize Medi-Cal and slash it by 10%.
Proposition 41 also deprives the state of flexibility to keep SB 125 effective in the
future. As enacted, the SB 125 tax uses up capacity under the Gann limit, narrowing room
for other revenue needs. SB 125 also sunsets in 2030, at a time when there might not be
room under the Gann limit available for renewal. In both cases, the state could be left
choosing between crowding out other priorities under the limit or losing the tax—and the

In addition, in 2024, Proposition 35 implemented a permanent MCO tax starting in
2027.13 Proposition 35 also used a provision of the Gann limit, Art. XIIIB, Sec. 4, to lift the

Threats to the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee (HQAF)
Prop 41 could also bar modifications to the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee (HQAF),
including modifications that might be required by the federal government in order for the
HQAF to remain in effect. The HQAF draws down billions of dollars in federal matching
funds for hospital payments, and the federal government approved the 2025 program in
June 2026. HQAF funds are exempt from the Gann limit.16 A court might conclude that an
HQAF modified after January 1, 2026 “takes effect” after that date for purposes of Prop 41.
That would prevent California from modifying or improving the HQAF, even if required by
federal rule changes, such as those now pending. A Trump or other hostile HHS aware of
this dilemma might go out of its way to require HQAF changes that it knows California
cannot implement.17
We expect that California would argue the HQAF is not subject to Prop 41 limits
because it is a “fee,” not a “tax,” but a court might well rule otherwise. This is because
Proposition 41 does not define “state tax” and because California generally interprets
“taxes” quite broadly. See Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(b). A multibillion dollar charge that funds not
only services for the payors but also transfers to others, as the HQAF does, will be quite
likely to face a plausible challenge that it constitutes a tax and not a fee.
Note that the stakes of these threats are further magnified because the statute
makes it so that the hospital fee becomes inoperative if a lawsuit is filed and a preliminary

Threats to the Skilled Nursing Facility Fees
Yet another health funding source at risk from Proposition 41 is the skilled nursing
facility quality assurance fee (SNF-QAF). Like the HQAF, this is a provision intended to

Proposition 41: Audits For New State Special Taxes
Proposition 41: Audits For New State Special Taxes
Proposition 41: Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits For New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Tax Audits, One-Time Wealth Tax for State-Funded Health Care Programs Initiative.
Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026
The Transparency Act
Summary
Proposition 41 was placed on the ballot by petition signatures to amend the California Constitution. It began as Initiative #25-0041A (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0040A1%20%28Gov.%20Efficiency%29.pdf) , filed with the California Attorney General’s Office. Prop. 41 amends the California Constitution by adding Article XXIV, creating audit review requirements for special tax measures and enforcing state appropriation limits (the Gann Limit) for all future state tax measures.
Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to conduct a financial and performance audit of any citizen initiative proposing a new special tax once the campaign collects 25% of required signatures. The auditor must review specific criteria set by Proposition 41, including identifying ways to cut the proposed program’s annual costs by 10%. If the measure qualifies, an executive summary of the audit is published in the official voter information pamphlet.
Additionally, the State Auditor will conduct ongoing audits every four years for programs receiving funding from special taxes created or increased by the Legislature or voters after January 1, 2026.
Proposition 41 specifies that the costs of these audits will be reimbursed using revenue generated from the new tax if voters approve the measure. If a special tax initiative fails, the state general fund covers the audit costs.
It would also prohibit the state from enforcing any new tax enacted or effective on or after January 1, 2026, that is exempted or excluded from the state spending limit.
Proposition 41 conflicts directly with Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm) (the Billionaire Wealth Tax initiative). If both pass, whichever measure receives more "yes" votes will prevail in its entirety. Because Proposition 40 excludes its revenues from the state spending limit, Proposition 41 would render Proposition 40 unenforceable if Proposition 41 wins more votes.
Note about the Gann Limit: Approved by California voters in 1979 asProposition 4 (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/ca_ballot_props/864/), the Gann Limit restricts how much tax revenue state and local governments (including school districts) can spend each year, adjusted annually for population changes and economic growth. The limit applies to both General Fund taxes (unrestricted funds for general government operations) and special taxes (funds earmarked for specific purposes), though certain spending categories—such as infrastructure and emergency response—are exempt. (Sources: California Budget Center, What is the Gann Limit? (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians) , Gann Limit (Wikipedia) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gann_Limit) , CA Department of Finance, Description of (https://dof.ca.gov/media/docs/budget/california-budget-frequently-asked-questions/fundclassifications.pdf)Fund Classifications in the Treasury (https://dof.ca.gov/media/docs/budget/california-budget-frequently-asked-questions/fundclassifications.pdf))
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. However, the State Auditor costs will increase due to the new and ongoing work to carry out the audit requirements in this measure.
Due to additional pages of audit information being included in the voter information guides could increase state printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative on the ballot.
What your vote means (LAO Analysis)
YES: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.

Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 41 improves transparency and reduces government waste by requiring independent state audits of programs funded by new special taxes while ensuring all state taxes respect voter-approved spending caps, as detailed in the Official Voter Information Guide.
Opponents contend that the measure was put on the ballot by billionaire opponents to block Prop. 40, a proposed wealth tax on billionaires, and that its audit requirements create unnecessary hurdles to funding essential public services like healthcare and education.
